source.title: Stronger Universal and Transferable Attacks by Suppressing Refusals
source.authors: David Huang; Avidan Shah; Alexandre Araujo; David A. Wagner; Chawin Sitawarin

page_placements.theme: Jailbreak mechanisms: suppressing the refusal direction, direction-guided attacks, and routes outside the single-turn direction

record.tranche_reason: The study calculates difference-in-means refusal vectors and directly removes their projections from model activations, reporting harmful-response rates; it describes this ablation evaluation as using the previously published method.
record.gate_note: The direct ablation outcomes, IRIS attack results with a GCG comparison, and the reported activation-similarity change are included. Values used to select a vector layer or tune beta are not results. Broader IRIS attack-rate evaluations in Tables 2, 3 and 7 are not included because they report end-to-end attack performance rather than a separate measurement of refusal-direction mediation. The study does not report adding a direction to induce refusals on harmless requests or testing general capability after ablation.
record.test_reason: Most of the paper is an attack (IRIS) that uses the refusal direction as a tool (T4-like). Appendix C, however, reports direct difference-in-means projection ablation following Arditi et al. It gives harmful-response rates on Llama-3-8B-Instruct (94%) and on the circuit-breaker variant Llama-3-RR using the Llama-3 vector (94%). These are T1 results on V1, and on V6 for one model variant.
record.authors_conclusion: Partly right. The authors' main conclusions are twofold. First, suffixes optimized on a single behavior and a single model are often inherently universal and transferable. Second, adding a refusal-direction suppression objective (IRIS) makes such suffixes much stronger, including against circuit-breaker models and frontier and reasoning models. The direct-ablation results (94% on Llama-3 and on Llama-3-RR) are reported only briefly in an appendix.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a difference-in-means refusal vector and direct projection ablation in its evaluation, but primarily adds a refusal-direction penalty to an adversarial suffix optimization objective rather than testing ablation and addition as a complete causal account.
record.method_sensitivity: Direct-ablation ASR varies from 0% to 100% across layer and vector-calculation choices. The study also reports that system prompts substantially affect ASR and that the judge can miss some IRIS-induced harmful responses.

fits_no_version.finding: Adding a loss that penalizes the refusal-direction projection to GCG/AutoDAN raises jailbreak success and suffix transferability. Examples: Llama-3 white-box 2%→58%, Vicuna transfer 12%→82%. Successful IRIS suffixes also drive cosine similarity with the refusal vector down to the level of harmless prompts.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Optimizing adversarial suffixes to suppress the refusal direction yields stronger, more universal and transferable jailbreaks. This holds even against circuit-breaker models and black-box frontier models.

record.peer_reviewed: North American Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics, 2025
record.problems: The direct-ablation range is not broken down by layer or vector calculation method. The reported ablation results do not include a stated unablated baseline or a general-capability evaluation. The cosine-similarity result is qualitative and figure-only. The paper notes limitations in LLM-judge accuracy, including false negatives for IRIS responses.
record.rows_left_out: Tables 2, 3 and 7 and other broader IRIS attack-rate evaluations are omitted: they report end-to-end attack performance, not separate measurements of refusal-direction mediation. The direct mechanism results and the Table 1 IRIS + GCG comparison are retained.

untested.parts: Adding the direction to induce refusal on harmless prompts; preservation of other capabilities after ablation; models beyond Llama-3-8B-Instruct and its RR variant.
Whether existing jailbreaks (GCG, AutoDAN, SCAV) suppress the direction; training against direction ablation for robustness.
Cross-language transfer, base-to-instruct transfer, and model variants other than circuit-breaker Llama-3-RR.
Reasoning models are only attacked with transferred suffixes; no direction measurement or ablation.

record.verdict_notes: Only the appendix ablation numbers bear directly on the claim; the attack-performance rows are own-method comparisons and are relinked to none. The Fig. 8 suppression result is by construction, since the suffixes are optimized for it, so it is not credited to V3. Ablation reporting is thin: no unablated baseline, no per-layer breakdown, and a mis-cited table. The judge is LlamaGuard-2, and the authors note false negatives.

versions.untested_parts: Does not test adding the direction to harmless requests or measure whether other abilities remain intact; ablation outcomes vary across vector and layer choices.
No weight-edit or released-model abliteration evaluation.
Does not test training against direction ablation for robustness; the activation-similarity result is qualitative.
No comparison of a single direction with an affine, cone, or multi-direction account.
Does not separate harmfulness judgment from the refusal decision.
Tests transfer of an ablation vector from Llama-3 to Llama-3-RR only; no language, base-to-instruct, or broader model-variant transfer tests.
Does not vary refusal-training method or timing.
Reports attacks on reasoning models, but does not test whether their refusals are mediated by the direction through ablation or another direct causal measure.

relation.reason: Its own ablation results (Appendix C, C.2) bear on V1 and V6.

tranche.reason: Most of the paper uses the direction as an attack tool (T4). Appendix C, however, reports its own difference-in-means projection ablation following Arditi et al., with harmful-response ASR on Llama-3-8B-Instruct (94%) and on Llama-3-RR (94%). That is the same method and a comparable measure.

source_check.notes: The ablation evidence is two appendix passages (C, C.2) with no unablated baseline, no random-direction control, no layer and no capability check. The Llama-3 94% probably comes after choosing the best layer (Section 5.1). There is no V3 verdict, which is right: Figure 8 shows the drop only for suffixes optimized to cause it, and no other attack is measured.
